explanations.explanation: That's it, baker. The elders and judges measure from the victim to the neighboring cities, and then the elders of the city nearest the victim take the heifer (Deuteronomy 21:2-3). Nobody gets to say "not my town." The measuring tape settles it.

explanations.answer: The largest town in the land
explanations.explanation: Big town energy, I like it, but size doesn't decide anything here. The elders and judges measure the distance from the victim to the neighboring cities, and the elders of the nearest one take the heifer (Deuteronomy 21:2-3). It's distance, not population. Even the biggest town in the land can't pull rank on a tape measure.

explanations.answer: The town where the man lived
explanations.explanation: Good thought, friend, but the text never says where he lived. Nobody even knows who killed him. What it says is that the elders measure to the neighboring cities, and the nearest one's elders take the heifer (Deuteronomy 21:2-3). So the measuring decides it.

explanations.answer: God chose them to serve and rule on cases
explanations.explanation: Right on, baker. Moses says the priests, the sons of Levi, come forward because "…the LORD your God has chosen them to serve Him and pronounce blessings in His name and to give a ruling in every dispute and case of assault." They aren't there by accident. God picked them for this.

explanations.answer: They live in the city nearest the field
explanations.explanation: Nice guess, but Moses never says where the priests live. He gives God's choice as the reason: "…the LORD your God has chosen them to serve Him and pronounce blessings in His name and to give a ruling in every dispute and case of assault." So they come forward because of that choosing, not their address.

explanations.answer: They were the ones who found the victim
explanations.explanation: Whoa, friend, slow down. That would make the priests part of the mystery, and the text never says they found anyone. Moses says they come forward because "…the LORD your God has chosen them to serve Him and pronounce blessings in His name and to give a ruling in every dispute and case of assault." They're there by God's choice, not as the finders.

Close, but it's False. The elders declare, "Our hands did not shed this blood, nor did our eyes see it." They say their eyes did not see it, so they're not claiming to be witnesses. If they had said they saw it, we'd have a whole different case on our hands. Moses tells them to say this while they wash their hands over the heifer (Deuteronomy 21:6 and 21:7).

That's right, baker. The elders declare, "Our hands did not shed this blood, nor did our eyes see it." They say it out loud, standing at the stream with their hands washed over the heifer. So no, they don't claim to have seen who killed the man. Say it with me: their eyes did not see it.

Yes, baker. Right after the elders pray, "Accept this atonement, O LORD, for Your people Israel whom You have redeemed…" Moses says, "And the bloodshed will be atoned for." That's the promise of the passage (Deuteronomy 21:8). It's settled.

It's actually True, friend. After the elders ask the LORD to accept this atonement, Moses says, "And the bloodshed will be atoned for." The text states it plainly (Deuteronomy 21:8). Easy one to second-guess, so don't feel bad.
Yep, guilt. Moses says, "So you shall purge from among you the guilt of shedding innocent blood…" The innocent blood is why this whole ceremony exists. Good work, baker.

Good try, friend, but memory isn't the word. Moses says Israel purges "…the guilt of shedding innocent blood…" The text doesn't say the memory gets erased. It names the guilt as what gets purged from among them.

I see why fear came to mind, baker. A killing nobody can solve would shake a town. But Moses says, "So you shall purge from among you the guilt of shedding innocent blood…" The word is guilt, not fear.
That's right, baker. Moses says, "…since you have done what is right in the eyes of the LORD." Israel follows the steps, and the LORD sees it as right. That's a good word to hear.

Actually it's True, friend. Moses says that when they do this, "…you have done what is right in the eyes of the LORD." The text gives them the thumbs up. I'd say that's a good word for Israel to hear after all those steps with the heifer and the stream.

Careful, baker, it's False. Moses says the man "…must not sell her for money or treat her as a slave…" If he isn't pleased with her, he's to let her go wherever she wishes. Selling her is off the table.

That's right, baker. Moses says, "…you are to let her go wherever she wishes. But you must not sell her for money or treat her as a slave…" Heavy topic, but the text is clear that she isn't to be sold.
Exactly. Moses says the man must not sell her or treat her as a slave, "…since you have dishonored her." That's the reason the text gives, and I won't add a thing to it. Well done, baker.

explanations.answer: She came from a royal family
explanations.explanation: Interesting guess, but Moses never says a word about her family being royal. The reason he gives is short: "…since you have dishonored her." That's the whole reason the text states.

explanations.answer: Her people might come for her
explanations.explanation: I get the thinking, friend, but the text doesn't say anything about her people coming for her. Moses says the man must not sell her for money or treat her as a slave, and he gives one reason: "…since you have dishonored her." That's the reason the text states, and I won't add to it.

Yes, baker. Moses says the father "…must not appoint the son of the beloved wife as the firstborn over the son of the unloved wife." He must acknowledge the firstborn, the unloved wife's son. Who the father loves more doesn't change who came first.

It's True, friend. Moses says the father "…must not appoint the son of the beloved wife as the firstborn over the son of the unloved wife." The unloved wife's son keeps his place. Favorites don't get to rewrite the birth order.

explanations.answer: A double portion of all he has
explanations.explanation: You got it, baker! Moses says the father must acknowledge the firstborn "…by giving him a double portion of all that he has." And that son belongs to the wife called unloved. The father can't slide the firstborn's right over to the favorite's son (Deuteronomy 21:15–16). I think that's one family meeting where nobody gets to say "but I'm the favorite." The text says the right of the firstborn belongs to him, and that's the end of the discussion.

explanations.answer: The family house and all its land
explanations.explanation: Good guess, but the text doesn't say that. Moses says the father must give him "…a double portion of all that he has." That covers everything the father owns, not one prize piece of it.

explanations.answer: Half of all his flocks and herds
explanations.explanation: Half sounds generous, friend, but the text says more than that. Moses says the father gives "…a double portion of all that he has." It's about all he has, not just the flocks and herds.

explanations.answer: He's the first son born of his father's strength
explanations.explanation: That's it, baker. Moses says, "For that son is the firstfruits of his father’s strength; the right of the firstborn belongs to him." The reason is that he's the first son, not who his mother is.

explanations.answer: His mother asked the elders to give it to him
explanations.explanation: Nope, friend, the text never mentions the mother asking the elders for anything. Moses says, "For that son is the firstfruits of his father’s strength; the right of the firstborn belongs to him." The right comes from him being the firstfruits of his father's strength. That's the reason Moses gives.

explanations.answer: He has always been the strongest of the sons
explanations.explanation: Sneaky one, because the word strength is in the verse. But Moses says, "For that son is the firstfruits of his father’s strength…" That's about being the first son of his father's strength, not about who is the strongest.

explanations.answer: He is a glutton and a drunkard
explanations.explanation: That's right, baker. The parents tell the elders, "This son of ours is stubborn and rebellious; he does not obey us. He is a glutton and a drunkard." It's a heavy section, so I'll just say that plainly and move on.

explanations.answer: He has stolen from his neighbors
explanations.explanation: The text doesn't say anything about stealing, friend. The parents say, "This son of ours is stubborn and rebellious; he does not obey us. He is a glutton and a drunkard." That's the charge they bring to the elders.

explanations.answer: He has lied to the whole city
explanations.explanation: Not quite, baker. Nothing in the text mentions lying to the city. The parents say, "He is a glutton and a drunkard." right after they say he doesn't obey them (Deuteronomy 21:20).
Yes, evil. Moses says, "So you must purge the evil from among you, and all Israel will hear and be afraid." Good catch, baker. It's a heavy line, and the word fits it.
I see why shame came up, friend, but that's not the word Moses uses. He says, "So you must purge the evil from among you…" The text names evil as the thing to purge.
Sorrow fits the mood, baker, and I think this passage is a sad one. But Moses says, "So you must purge the evil from among you…" The word in the text is evil.
Careful, baker, it's False. Moses says, "…all Israel will hear and be afraid." The text says Israel hears about it, not that it's kept quiet.
That's right, baker. Moses says, "…all Israel will hear and be afraid." The word spreads, which is the opposite of keeping it quiet.

Right, baker. Moses says, "…you must not leave the body on the tree overnight, but you must be sure to bury him that day…" No overnight stay is allowed. The burial happens that very day. Moses also says the land is something the LORD is giving them as an inheritance, and they must not defile it (Deuteronomy 21:23).

explanations.answer: Leave it up for three days
explanations.explanation: Not quite, friend. Moses says, "…you must not leave the body on the tree overnight…" That rules out even one night, never mind three days. The body is to be buried that day.

explanations.answer: Keep it up until the elders say
explanations.explanation: Good thought, but the text gives a different deadline. Moses says, "…you must not leave the body on the tree overnight, but you must be sure to bury him that day…" He doesn't mention waiting for the elders at all. The text sets the time: that same day.
Yes, baker. Moses says, "…because anyone who is hung on a tree is under God’s curse." That's why the body can't stay up overnight. It's a solemn line, and I'll leave it as the text gives it.
I understand the thought, friend, but protection isn't the word. Moses says, "…because anyone who is hung on a tree is under God’s curse." The text uses the word curse.
Mercy is a lovely word, baker, but it's not the one Moses uses here. He says, "…because anyone who is hung on a tree is under God’s curse." The word in the text is curse.
